sections.title: Margin & Growth
sections.subtitle: The investment thesis: operating earnings margin hit a record 14.5% in FY2026 while revenue fell for the second straight year -- this is a margin/deleveraging story, not a growth story

charts.title: Operating Earnings Margin (record high on falling revenue)
charts.annotation: H1 2026 sits at 7.9% (seasonally the weaker half); full-year FY2026 closed at 14.5%, a record, despite revenue declining from 56.6m to 55.2m.

charts.title: Revenue vs Operating Earnings (EBITDA before significant items)
Net Income (NPAT)
charts.annotation: FY2024's +0.65m came from a deferred-tax BENEFIT over a pre-tax LOSS of -2.858m. FY2026's +1.3m NPAT (1.7c EPS) is also not fully cash-taxed -- management grosses it up to a 'cash equivalent' ~1.8m using carried-forward tax losses. Four of the last five years were losses.

sections.title: Deleveraging & Balance Sheet
sections.subtitle: Bank debt and covenant leverage falling steadily -- the second thesis pillar and the gate for the first-ever dividend

charts.title: Total Debt & Cash

sections.title: Owner Cash Flow & Hospitality Operations
sections.subtitle: Why headline free cash flow overstates what owners actually keep, and the venue-level drivers of the business

charts.title: Reported FCF vs Owner FCF (after lease principal & interest)
charts.annotation: Savor is an IFRS-16 lessee across 18 venues: lease principal (~NZ$3.05m in FY2025) and lease interest (~NZ$0.72m) both sit in financing cash flow, so reported FCF (NZ$5.98m FY2025) overstates what owners actually keep by ~NZ$3.8m a year. Owner FCF was NEGATIVE FY2021-23 during the venue build-out and only turned positive in FY2024-25; FY2026's estimated 0.55m is a capex-elevated trough (Bar Ziti and Flush Golf fit-outs), not the run rate.

charts.title: Operating Cash Flow vs CapEx
charts.annotation: FY2026 capex not yet disclosed (results release only); DCF model estimates ~NZ$2.4m, elevated versus NZ$0.3-1.3m in FY2024-25 for the two new Britomart venues.

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Total sales across all venues: dine-in food & beverage (~85%), private events/functions (~10%), the Flush Golf entertainment format (~3%) and Oji wholesale/grab-and-go (~2%). Recognised at point of sale, so it is transactional, not recurring.

For Savor: revenue has now declined two years running (NZ$61.9m → NZ$56.6m → NZ$55.2m) as discretionary dining spend came under cost-of-living pressure, even as two new venues opened in FY2026.

What to watch:

  • Whether the two new Britomart venues (Bar Ziti, Flush Golf, opened Sep-2025) offset the like-for-like decline as they mature through their first 12 months
  • Over 65% of Group earnings are historically generated in the Nov-Mar summer trading months -- a single soft summer can determine the whole year
  • City Rail Link opening (13-Sep-2026) next to the Britomart cluster as a potential foot-traffic tailwind

operatingMargin.title: Operating Earnings Margin
operatingMargin.content:
EBITDA before significant items (impairment, restructuring) as a percentage of revenue -- management's headline guided metric.

For Savor: this is the single most important chart on this dashboard. Margin hit a record 14.5% in FY2026 while revenue FELL from 56.6m to 55.2m -- proof the story is cost discipline and mix (COGS below 28% of revenue, ~NZ$1m of venue-wage savings), not top-line growth. FY2025's -8% revenue took the margin from 14.2% (FY2024) down to 12.8% before FY2026's recovery to a new high.

What to watch:

  • Whether 14.5%+ margins hold if revenue keeps declining -- the high fixed-cost base (rent, wages) means further revenue softness could compress margin quickly (severe operating leverage)
  • H1 (winter, softer season) typically prints a much lower margin than the full year -- H1 2026 was 7.9%
  • The DCF's base case assumes only a modest further step-up to 15.5% headline margin, long-run, less a 1.25%-of-revenue recurring restructuring allowance

ebitda.title: Operating Earnings (EBITDA before significant items)
ebitda.content:
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, amortisation and significant/one-off items (impairment, restructuring costs) -- the company's own headline profitability measure, identical here to reported EBITDA.

For Savor: NZ$8.0m in FY2026, a new high, versus NZ$7.3m FY2025 and a NZ$8.8m FY2024 peak -- recovered past the prior peak on lower revenue, underscoring the margin story.

What to watch:

  • The gap to statutory operating income/NPAT: impairment (NZ$4.3m in FY2024) and restructuring costs (NZ$0.9-2.5m every year FY2021-25) are charged below this line every single year, so it is not a one-off exclusion
  • Conversion to operating cash flow has historically run 73-98%, not 100%

netIncome.title: Net Income (NPAT)
netIncome.content:
Statutory profit after tax attributable to shareholders.

For Savor: NPAT has been NEGATIVE in four of the last five years despite growing operating earnings, because impairments, restructuring costs and interest sit below the EBITDA line. FY2024's apparent +0.65m profit was actually a deferred-tax BENEFIT recognised over a pre-tax LOSS of -2.858m -- read the tax line, not just the headline. FY2026's +1.3m (1.7c EPS) is similarly boosted: only part is cash tax, and management itself grosses it up to a “cash equivalent” ~1.8m using carried-forward tax losses (~NZ$26.7m at FY2025).

What to watch:

  • Whether tax losses (which shelter cash tax) get forfeited on any future ownership change or recapitalisation -- the DCF assumes a faster tax ramp than the losses strictly require, for exactly this reason
  • NPAT swings from small profit to loss on modest revenue moves -- high operating leverage

debt.title: Total Debt & Cash
debt.content:
Bank borrowings (the CSV's TotalDebt column) and cash on the balance sheet. Excludes IFRS-16 lease liabilities, which are shown separately in the deleveraging narrative and treated as an operating cost, not debt, in the DCF.

For Savor: bank debt peaked near NZ$14.6m in 2021-22 during the venue-expansion phase and has been paid down steadily since -- NZ$9.0m at FY2025, an estimated ~NZ$8.0m at FY2026 (1.92x covenant leverage), and a further NZ$0.5m repaid in April 2026 (to 1.80x, ~1.4x net of cash). This deleveraging is the second half of the investment thesis alongside the margin story.

What to watch:

  • The 1.5x leverage trigger for the company's promised first-ever dividend (targeted January 2027) -- needs roughly a further NZ$0.75m of bank repayment by December 2026, out of a winter half that historically burns cash
  • FY2026 figures here are estimates from the results release pending the audited annual report

equity.title: Shareholders' Equity vs Total Liabilities
equity.content:
Book equity and total liabilities (bank debt + lease liabilities + trade/other payables) from the balance sheet.

For Savor: equity grew from NZ$12.7m (FY2021) to NZ$18.8m (FY2024) partly on a NZ$3.5m deferred-tax asset recognition and a share issue, not retained earnings -- book value growth has diverged from the loss-making earnings history and should not be read as organic compounding.

What to watch:

  • FY2026 balance sheet is not yet published (results-release basis only) -- this chart stops at FY2025
  • Liabilities include ~NZ$17-18m of lease liabilities across 18 venues, a large fixed commitment relative to NZ$17-19m of equity

eps.title: Earnings Per Share
eps.content:
Basic EPS in NZ cents.

For Savor: the axis is CENTS -- FY2026's 1.7c is NZ$0.017/share, not NZ$1.70. FY2021's -13.9c predates the 1-for-3 share consolidation of 9-August-2021 (146.3m shares before, ~48-77m after), so it is not comparable to later years on a per-share basis; treat FY2022 onward as the comparable history.

What to watch:

  • EPS has been negative in four of the last five years; FY2024 and FY2026's positive prints both rely on tax benefits/gross-ups rather than fully cash-taxed profit (see the Net Income note)

ownerFcf.title: Reported FCF vs Owner FCF (after lease cash)
ownerFcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capex, as filed. Owner FCF (from the DCF model) additionally deducts lease principal AND lease interest -- both of which IFRS 16 classifies inside financing cash flow for Savor, not operating, so they never touch reported OCF or reported FCF.

For Savor: this is the most important cash-flow chart on the dashboard. Reported FCF looks robust (NZ$5.98m FY2025, NZ$6.09m FY2024) but Savor pays roughly NZ$3.8m/year of lease cash (principal + interest) across 18 leased venues that is invisible in that number. True owner FCF was NEGATIVE every year FY2021-23 during the venue build-out, turned positive at ~NZ$2.0-2.2m in FY2024-25, and an estimated NZ$0.55m in FY2026 (a capex-elevated trough from the Bar Ziti/Flush Golf fit-outs, not the run rate).

What to watch:

  • Never read the reported-FCF bar as the cash available to shareholders or debt paydown -- use the owner FCF bar
  • The DCF discounts owner FCF, which is why the model's intrinsic value (NZ$0.135 base case) sits below the market price of NZ$0.172 despite a healthy-looking reported FCF yield

ocfCapex.title: Operating Cash Flow vs CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Cash generated from operations before financing items, and capital expenditure on venue fit-outs, equipment and maintenance (excludes lease principal, which is a financing item under IFRS 16).

For Savor: OCF has grown from NZ$0.4m (FY2021) to NZ$6.4-7.1m (FY2024-25) as the venue estate matured post-COVID. Capex was unusually low in FY2024-25 (NZ$0.3-1.1m) and stepped up in FY2026 (estimated ~NZ$2.4m) to fund the two new venues opened in September 2025.

What to watch:

  • This chart still excludes the ~NZ$3.8m/year of lease cash that sits in financing -- see the Owner FCF chart for the fuller picture of what the business actually retains

dcf.base_sublabel: Owner FCF — after lease principal & interest, before dividend
dcf.growth_hint: Base-case Year-1 revenue growth (CPI-like; FY2021-26 ramp was reopening/acquisition, not organic)
dcf.current_price_note: 3-Sep-2026 -- house model says OVERVALUED at this price on a probability-weighted basis
dcf.model_approach_note: Two things to hold in mind reading this section. First, the base-case intrinsic value of NZ$0.135 sits BELOW the current price of NZ$0.172 -- on a probability-weighted basis (NZ$0.123) the house model reads the stock as roughly 28% overvalued, even though it screens cheap on trailing multiples (FY2026 EV/EBITDA ~5.5x, P/E ~10.9x). The gap is a size/illiquidity/cyclicality premium the market is not charging: at NZ$0.172 the market is capitalising the promised January-2027 dividend at roughly 13.6-14.4%, well inside this model's 16.5% WACC. Second, the bear-case intrinsic value is NEGATIVE (-NZ$0.036/share): in the bear path, owner FCF of only NZ$0.5-0.7m/year does not cover the NZ$6.3m of net bank debt at a 16.5% discount rate. That is a real signal about a levered, single-city microcap with 65% of earnings concentrated in five summer months -- not a modelling artifact -- and limited liability floors the actual downside at zero.
